meta.title: Yoruba Alphabet
meta.subtitle: 34 letters, tones and sounds · both directions, as two cards each
meta.desc: The Latin alphabet in which Yoruba is written, and the marks on it: 34 notes — the 25 letters in the order Nigerian primers give them (A B D E Ẹ F G GB H I J K L M N O Ọ P R S Ṣ T U W Y; there is no c, q, v, x or z), then the three tones and the marks that write them, the five nasal vowels and the syllabic nasal. The first deck of the Yoruba collection. Both directions: see a letter or a mark and recall its sound, or see a sound and recall what writes it, each a card with its own schedule. Most letters sound as an English reader expects, and the cards say so in a line; the notes that matter are the ones English has no letter for — Ẹ and Ọ, the OPEN e and o, told from e and o by the dot beneath (a short vertical line in older printing); Ṣ, the sh of shop; GB and P, each ONE sound made with the tongue and the lips closed at once (Yoruba's p is never an English p); and the TONES, which are part of every word: an acute accent for a high tone (á), a grave for a low one (à), and no mark for a mid tone, so that ọkọ is 'husband', ọkọ̀ 'vehicle' and ọkọ́ 'hoe'. Every word in the collection's level decks carries its tone marks. Each card gives an everyday word that shows the sound, from the Yoruba A1 deck, with the meaning A1 gives it. The sounds are approximations, as every learner's alphabet gives them, for Standard Yoruba. There is no read-aloud button: few devices carry a Yoruba voice, and one without it reads the letter in English. Sources: the standard description of Standard Yoruba; the example words and their meanings are English Wiktionary's, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0).

fields.Sound: a CLOSE e, like the e of café or the ay of day without its glide into "ee"
an OPEN e, like the e of bet; the dot under it is what tells it from e
f, as in English
always the hard g of go — never the g of gem
ONE sound, a letter of its own: g and b said at the same moment, the back of the tongue and the lips closed together and opened together — no English word has it
h, as in English
the ee of see, short and pure
the j of jam, often softer, nearer the dg of judge
k, as in English
l, as in English; before a nasal vowel it is said n
m, as in English
n, as in English, at the start of a syllable; after a vowel in the same syllable it is not said, but marks the vowel as nasal (below)
a CLOSE o, like the o of so without its glide into "oo"
an OPEN o, like the o of British hot or the aw of law; the dot is what tells it from o
NOT an English p: gb's voiceless twin, k and p said at the same moment, the tongue and the lips closed together and opened together
a light tap of the tongue tip, like the r of Spanish pero
s, as in English — never the z sound of rose
the sh of shop; the dot under it is what tells it from s
t, as in English
the oo of food, short and pure
w, as in English
the y of yes
a HIGH tone: the voice held high on the syllable
a MID tone: the voice level, in the middle of its range; most writing leaves it unmarked, and so do these decks
a LOW tone: the voice held low on the syllable
a NASAL a, said through the nose with no n sound after it; many speakers say it as ọn
a NASAL ẹ, the e of bet said through the nose; it is found in very few words, ìyẹn "that" the commonest
a NASAL i, the ee of see said through the nose
a NASAL ọ, the aw of law said through the nose: how the nasal a is said after b, f, w, gb and p, and written so there (àwọn); after m no n is written at all (mi, mu)
a NASAL u, the oo of food said through the nose
a SYLLABIC NASAL: an n (m before b) that is a syllable of its own, with its own tone mark — a hum, with no vowel
